pairs.subject: subprocess-lifecycle
pairs.evidence: crates/table-engine/src/native.rs:252 Every way a run can end (cancel, total timeout, normal finish, error) closes the kill-on-close job straight away. The whole tree is killed with no polite stop, no grace deadline and no record of which rung ended it, so the termination ladder exists only as its final rung.

techniques.evidence: crates/table-engine/src/native.rs:252 Several parts are realized: a kernel job binding attached while the child is still suspended (windows_job.rs), kill_on_drop, an unconditional child.wait() after the kill, and distinct Spawn/Attach/Exit{code}/Timeout/Cancelled errors. The ladder itself is missing: no polite stop, no grace deadline, and the rung used is never recorded.

crates/table-engine/src/native.rs:248 A cancel races the run and is enforced by killing the job/process tree, a unit the host can survive losing. No cooperative token is relied on. The signalled-vs-reaped counts are not emitted.

crates/table-engine/src/native.rs:207 The time-to-first-contact deadline is separate and arms correctly (line 205). After Init, though, reads wait without bound until the 120s total ceiling. There is no activity record per run, no stalled state and no degraded claim.

crates/table-engine/src/native.rs:178 Every run gets a default ceiling (RunLimits 10s init / 120s total), and output is budgeted at 4 MiB total and 64 KiB per line. But nothing samples memory or CPU pressure before the spawn, there is no memory budget on the job, and Error::Timeout does not record the ceiling's value.
crates/table-engine/src/native.rs:170 Every run is a deliberate cold, ephemeral spawn with a fresh per-run session uuid. There is no warm pool or resumable session to fingerprint.

crates/table-engine/src/native.rs:423 The output is a declared-UTF-8 JSONL protocol stream, decoded strictly by that declaration (an invalid line is an error, not a lossy guess). The technique's own carve-out covers this case. stderr is drained and dropped.
